packs.title: People and places
packs.blurb: Who is around you and where things are: family and neighbours, rooms and streets, the weather, and the two untranslatable words Dutch people use constantly.

entries.pattern: A de-word. The female form is `de vriendin`, and both can mean a partner in context.

examples.nl: Ik ga met een vriend naar de film.
examples.en: I am going to the cinema with a friend.

entries.pitfall: `mijn vriend` usually means boyfriend. For a plain friend say `een vriend van mij`.

entries.pattern: A de-word, built from `buur` plus `man`. The female form is `de buurvrouw`.

examples.nl: De buurvrouw neemt het pakje aan.
examples.en: The neighbour takes in the parcel.

entries.hook: `de buurt` is the neighbourhood and `de buren` the neighbours. One root, three words you need.

entries.pattern: A het-word, and a distinction English does not make.

examples.nl: Wij zijn een gezin van vier.
examples.en: We are a household of four.
My extended family lives in India.

entries.pitfall: `het gezin` is the household you live in. `de familie` is the wider family. Using familie for your own household sounds odd.

entries.pattern: The fixed preposition is `met`, matching English, which makes this one of the easy ones.

examples.nl: Zij zijn al tien jaar getrouwd.
examples.en: They have been married for ten years.

entries.pattern: `eruit zien` is a separable verb, so `uit` lands at the end and `er` sits in front of it.

examples.nl: Hoe ziet je nieuwe huis eruit?
examples.en: What does your new house look like?

entries.hook: `Zij ziet er moe uit` is the pattern to own: subject, ziet, er, the adjective, then uit.

entries.pattern: `lang` covers both long and tall. Dutch does not separate them.

examples.nl: Het is maar een korte wandeling.
examples.en: It is only a short walk.

entries.hook: `Hoe lang?` can mean how tall or how long. Context decides, and nobody gets confused.

entries.pattern: A de-word with an irregular plural: de steden.

examples.nl: Welke steden ken je in Nederland?
examples.en: Which cities do you know in the Netherlands?

entries.hook: `naar de stad` means into town. For the actual city centre, Dutch says `het centrum`.

entries.pattern: A de-word. You live `in` a street in Dutch, not on it.
entries.pitfall: Dutch says `in de straat`, where English says on the street. The preposition does not transfer.

entries.pattern: A het-word. Any word ending in -um is a het-word, which is a reliable cue.

examples.nl: We spreken af in het centrum.
examples.en: We will meet in the centre.

entries.hook: Words ending in -um are always het-words: het centrum, het museum, het album. A rare dependable rule.

entries.pattern: Directions. `rechts` is right-hand; `rechtdoor` is straight on. The two look alike and mean different things.
entries.pitfall: `rechts` is right, `rechtdoor` is straight ahead. Mixing them up sends you the wrong way.

entries.pattern: A position preposition. Pairs with tegenover, tussen and achter.

examples.nl: De bakker zit naast de apotheek.
examples.en: The baker is next to the pharmacy.
I am sitting next to the window.

entries.hook: Learn the position set together: naast, tegenover, tussen, achter, voor. They answer every `waar` question.

entries.pattern: `ver` almost always travels with `weg` when it means far away.
entries.hook: `ver` on its own sounds incomplete in speech. Store `ver weg` as the chunk.

entries.pattern: A de-word, and the base of several compound nouns you will need when house-hunting.

examples.nl: Onze kamer is klein maar licht.
examples.en: Our room is small but light.

entries.hook: One root, four rooms: woonkamer, slaapkamer, badkamer, wachtkamer. Dutch builds words by sticking them together.

entries.pattern: A de-word. The `eu` is a rounded sound with no English equivalent.

examples.nl: Ik sta de hele dag in de keuken.
examples.en: I am in the kitchen all day.

entries.pattern: A de-word. `huren` is to rent from someone, `verhuren` to rent out.

examples.nl: De huur is elke maand hetzelfde.
examples.en: The rent is the same every month.

entries.hook: `de huurder` rents, `de verhuurder` rents out. The `ver-` flips who is doing what to whom.

entries.pattern: A het-word, and the safest small-talk topic in the country.
entries.pitfall: `weer` also means again. `Ik kom weer` is I am coming again, nothing to do with weather.

entries.pattern: Weather uses a dummy `het` as subject, exactly as English uses `it`.

examples.nl: Het regent al de hele dag.
examples.en: It has been raining all day.

examples.nl: Als het regent, neem ik de bus.
examples.en: If it rains, I take the bus.

entries.hook: One pattern, four kinds of weather: het regent, het waait, het vriest, het sneeuwt.

entries.pattern: An untranslatable Dutch favourite. It covers food, weather, sleep, and feeling well.
entries.hook: `lekker` is the single most Dutch word on this list. Food, weather, a nap and your health can all be lekker.
entries.pitfall: `Ik voel me niet lekker` means I feel unwell. It has nothing to do with taste.

entries.pattern: Famously untranslatable. It describes the warm feeling of good company, not a thing.
entries.hook: Dutch people use gezellig as a compliment about an evening, a room or a person. Using it correctly earns you a lot of goodwill.

entries.pattern: A pair worth learning together. `druk` describes both crowded places and busy people.

examples.nl: Het is druk in de winkel.
Ik heb het druk deze week.

entries.hook: `Ik heb het druk` needs the `het`. Without it the sentence is wrong.

packs.title: Doing things
packs.blurb: The high-frequency verbs in the chunks they actually live in, including the fixed prepositions and the pairs English merges into one word.

entries.pattern: The preposition depends on what follows: `bij` a company, `als` a job title, `in` a sector.
entries.hook: Three prepositions, three meanings: bij the employer, als the role, in the field.

entries.pattern: A fixed phrase with the preposition `in`. The everyday way to suggest anything.

examples.nl: Ik heb geen zin om te koken.
examples.en: I do not feel like cooking.

entries.hook: A noun takes `zin in`, a verb takes `zin om te`: zin in koffie, but zin om te koken.
entries.pitfall: This is how Dutch people invite you to things. A blunt `Wil je koffie?` is noticeably colder.

entries.pattern: A separable verb, so `af` flies to the end in a plain sentence.

examples.nl: We spreken om zes uur af.

entries.hook: `Afgesproken!` on its own means 'agreed, it is a deal'. A whole reply in one word.

entries.pattern: A separable verb. `op` goes to the end: `Ik haal je op`.

examples.nl: Ik haal je om acht uur op.
examples.en: I will pick you up at eight.
Could you pick up the children?

entries.pitfall: `afhalen` is for collecting a thing, often a takeaway. `ophalen` is for collecting a person.

entries.pattern: Separable again. Dutch is full of these, and the prefix always carries the meaning.
entries.hook: The participle wedges ge- into the middle: op + ge + beld.

entries.pattern: Dutch has no single verb for need. It uses an adjective plus hebben, and `nodig` goes near the end.
entries.hook: The order is object first, `nodig` last: `Ik heb een pen nodig`, never `Ik heb nodig een pen`.
entries.pitfall: This word order trips up almost every learner. Practise it as a frame.

entries.pattern: The two modals that decide obligation and permission. Both send the other verb to the end.

examples.en: Am I allowed to park here?

entries.hook: `moet niet` means must not, but Dutch often uses `hoeft niet` for 'need not'. The two are easy to confuse.

entries.pattern: `hoeven` appears almost only in the negative. It is the polite way to decline an offer.

examples.en: You do not have to come.

entries.hook: `Dat hoeft niet` is the standard way to wave off an offer kindly. Worth having ready.
entries.pitfall: `Je moet niet komen` means you must not come. `Je hoeft niet te komen` means you need not. Very different.

entries.gloss: to know (a fact) / to know (a person)
entries.pattern: English has one verb here and Dutch has two. Facts take weten, people and places take kennen.
entries.hook: If you could follow it with `that ...`, use weten. If it is a person, a place or a work, use kennen.
entries.pitfall: `Ik ken het niet` about a fact is wrong. The sentence you want is `Ik weet het niet`.

entries.pattern: Two meanings. With an opinion it means think; with an object it means find.

examples.en: What do you think of it?

examples.nl: Ik kan mijn sleutels niet vinden.

entries.hook: `Wat vind je ervan?` is the standard invitation to give an opinion. Learn it whole.

entries.gloss: to love, to be fond of
entries.pattern: The fixed preposition is `van`. Works for people and for things.
entries.hook: In speech the `d` drops: `Ik hou van`, not `Ik houd van`. Both are written, only one is spoken.

entries.pattern: The comparative of `graag`, and the easiest way to express a preference.

examples.nl: Ik ga liever met de fiets.
examples.en: I prefer to go by bike.

entries.hook: graag, liever, het liefst. Like good, better, best, but for how much you want something.

entries.pattern: A fixed pair. `beginnen` takes `zijn` in the perfect, which catches people out.

examples.en: We will start with lesson one.

entries.pitfall: Perfect tense is `is begonnen`, not `heeft begonnen`. It is a change-of-state verb, so it takes zijn.

entries.pattern: `klaar` means both ready and finished. The preposition `met` sorts out which.

examples.nl: Ik ben klaar met mijn werk.

examples.en: Are you ready? We are leaving.

entries.hook: `klaar met` is finished with. Plain `klaar` is ready. The preposition does the work.

entries.pattern: The classic fixed pair. English says wait for, Dutch fixes on op, and no logic connects them.

examples.en: I am waiting for the bus.

entries.pitfall: `wachten voor` is wrong, however natural it feels coming from English.

entries.pattern: Another fixed pair, and it sits in a family with kijken naar and zoeken naar.

examples.en: Listen to what I am saying.

entries.hook: The `naar` group travels together: luisteren, kijken, zoeken, vragen. Learn them as a set.

entries.pattern: A tiny softener with no English equivalent. It turns an order into a request.

examples.en: May I just have a look?

entries.hook: Dropping `even` into a request is the cheapest politeness upgrade in Dutch. `Kom hier` is an order; `Kom even hier` is a request.

entries.pattern: Does two jobs: the adjective 'ordinary' and a filler meaning 'just'.

examples.nl: Ik wilde het gewoon even vragen.

entries.hook: `Doe maar gewoon, dan doe je al gek genoeg` is a national saying: act normal, that is odd enough already. It tells you a lot about Dutch culture.

entries.pattern: A de-word. `de cursus` is the whole course, `de les` one session of it.

examples.nl: De les begint om tien uur.

examples.en: I am taking a Dutch course.

entries.hook: You `volg` a course in Dutch, you do not take or do one: `een cursus volgen`.

entries.pattern: The verb you will use about your own learning more than any other.

examples.nl: Ik oefen elke dag een beetje.
examples.en: I practise a little every day.
We are going to practise pronunciation.

entries.hook: `het oefenexamen` is a practice exam. You will meet that word a lot on DUO's website.
